title: Tariff incidence reaches consumers through direct import prices and slower domestic supply-chain markups
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35561; U.S. 2025 tariff episode, consumer prices, imported inputs, and domestic producer markups
geography: United States goods markets and supply chains

observations.period: 2025 U.S. tariff episode; paper issued July 2026

denominator.unit: tariff-exposed and less-exposed goods and supply-chain price observations; public abstract does not disclose the full observation count

consumer_price_pass_through.unit: percent of the tariff increase passed through to consumer prices relative to less-exposed goods, holding aggregate conditions fixed

direct_share.unit: percent of the consumer-price increase attributed to direct effects on foreign varieties

indirect_share.unit: percent attributed to imported-input costs and domestic-producer markup responses

indirect_lag.unit: reported supply-chain transmission delay for indirect effects

observations.method: NBER empirical analysis of the 2025 U.S. tariffs comparing exposed and less-exposed goods, decomposing direct import-price effects from imported-input and domestic-markup channels while holding aggregate conditions fixed.
observations.uncertainty: This is a working paper and the abstract does not disclose all sample construction details. The estimate is relative to less-exposed goods and does not identify every household’s burden, substitution, wage response, or welfare effect.
observations.subgroup: Tariff-exposed goods, foreign varieties, domestic producers using imported inputs, and consumers over different transmission horizons.
observations.counterinterpretation: The delayed indirect channel may reflect supply-chain adjustment and market power rather than a uniform consumer price response; firms and households can also substitute products, suppliers, or locations.

boundary: This record adds a trade-to-consumer mechanism: geopolitical trade policy can redistribute costs through both rapid import prices and delayed domestic supply-chain markups. It does not show household hardship, political attribution, firm exit, or whether the policy achieved its strategic objective.
